items.stem: What is meant by corrosion?

options.text: The destruction of materials by chemical reactions with the environment
Damage suffered only by metals, caused by oxygen in the air
The rusting of iron that has been left outside in the wet
The wearing away of a surface by scratching, rubbing and use

items.why: This is the specification definition: corrosion is the destruction of materials by chemical reactions with substances in the environment.

items.stem: Which conditions are necessary for iron to rust?

options.text: Water alone; the air around the iron plays no part in it
Both air and water in contact with the iron surface
Air alone, since rust is simply an oxide of iron
Salt water only, as pure water cannot rust iron

items.why: The specification states that both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.

items.stem: A nail is put in a tube of water that has been boiled and then covered with a layer of oil. After a week the nail has not rusted. What does this show?

options.text: The layer of oil is what stopped the nail rusting here
Rusting needs only air, so the water was never needed
Water on its own cannot rust iron, so air is needed
A week is not long enough for rusting to be seen

items.why: Boiling drives dissolved air out and the oil stops it returning. The nail has water but no air and does not rust, so air is necessary as well.

items.stem: A nail is sealed in a tube of air with anhydrous calcium chloride at the bottom. After a week it has not rusted. What does this show?

options.text: Calcium chloride is a chemical that prevents rust
Air plays no part in the rusting of iron at all
Sealing up the tube is what kept the nail shiny here
Dry air cannot rust iron, so water is needed

items.why: The calcium chloride removes water vapour, so the nail has air but no water. It does not rust, so water is necessary as well.

items.stem: Which method prevents corrosion by acting as a barrier?

options.text: Painting the surface so that air and water cannot reach the metal
Bolting blocks of magnesium along the outside of the pipe
Heating the metal strongly to harden its outside layer
Mixing carbon into the metal to turn it into an alloy

items.why: Greasing, painting and electroplating are the barrier methods named by the specification; they keep air and water off the surface.

items.stem: Aluminium is a reactive metal, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode away. Why not?

options.text: Aluminium is unreactive, so nothing in the air can attack it
An oxide coating forms that protects the metal underneath
Its oxide flakes away, leaving fresh clean metal behind
Frames are always painted before they are fitted

items.why: Aluminium has an oxide coating that protects the metal from further corrosion.

items.stem: Iron sheets are galvanised. What does this mean?

options.text: They are coated with tin, a metal that resists corrosion
They are dipped in acid to clean them before painting
They are coated with zinc, which is more reactive
They are melted together with zinc as an alloy

items.why: Galvanising is coating iron with zinc, a more reactive metal that gives sacrificial protection.

items.stem: A galvanised bucket is scratched right through to the iron. Why does the iron still not rust?

options.text: The zinc melts and seals the scratch up again
The iron corrodes first and so protects the zinc
The scratch is too narrow for water to get into
The zinc corrodes away in place of the iron

items.why: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead: sacrificial protection works even where the coating is broken.

items.stem: Blocks of metal are bolted to a steel ship's hull to give sacrificial protection. Which metal should be used?

options.text: Magnesium, as it is more reactive than iron and corrodes first
Copper, because it is less reactive and resists corrosion
Tin, because it sits below iron and will not be eaten away
Lead, because it is dense and very heavy for its size

items.why: Sacrificial protection needs a metal above iron in the reactivity series, so it reacts in the iron's place.

items.stem: Why are most metals in everyday use alloys rather than pure metals?

options.text: Alloys are compounds, so they cannot react with air at all
The mixture has properties, like hardness, that suit the job
Mixing metals always makes them much softer and easier to bend
Pure metals cost far too much to make in large amounts

items.why: Most metals in everyday use are alloys because mixing gives more useful properties than the pure metal has.

items.stem: Which statement about bronze is correct?

options.text: It is copper mixed with zinc in fixed amounts
It is a compound formed from copper and tin
It is an alloy of copper mixed with tin
It is a pure metal mined as bronze ore

items.why: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.

items.stem: Brass is used for musical instruments and door fittings. What is brass?

options.text: A mixture of copper and pure tin
A compound of copper and zinc
Iron with a thin copper coating
A mixture of copper and zinc

items.why: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, which is why it is used for instruments and fittings.

items.stem: Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy. Which metals is the gold usually mixed with?

options.text: The gold is mixed with silver, copper and zinc
Nothing else, since jewellery gold is pure
Iron and carbon, added to harden the gold
A compound of gold, silver, copper and zinc

items.why: Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc.

items.stem: A ring is stamped 18 carat. What does this tell you about the ring?

options.text: It contains 18% gold and 82% of other metals
It is 75% gold, because 24 carat means pure gold
It is pure gold and it weighs 18 carats on a balance
It has 18 parts of gold to 24 parts of other metal

items.why: Carats are measured out of 24, so 18 carat is 18/24, which is 75% gold.

items.stem: How does high carbon steel differ from low carbon steel?

options.text: High carbon steel is soft and easy to shape; low carbon steel is brittle
High carbon steel resists corrosion; low carbon steel rusts very fast
High carbon steel is strong but brittle; low carbon steel is softer
High carbon steel is a compound; low carbon steel is a mixture

items.why: High carbon steel is strong but brittle, while low carbon steel is softer and more easily shaped.

items.stem: Why is stainless steel chosen for cutlery and sinks?

options.text: It is pure iron, so there is nothing to rust
It has extra carbon in it, which stops any rust
It is soft, so it can be pressed into thin sheets
It is hard and it resists corrosion well

items.why: Steels containing chromium and nickel are hard and resistant to corrosion.

items.stem: Aluminium alloys are used for the bodies of aircraft. Which property makes them suitable?

options.text: They are low density, so a given volume of them weighs less
They are the strongest metals known, so they never bend
They are dense, so they are tough enough for an aircraft.
They melt easily, so parts can be cast into shape

items.why: Aluminium alloys are low density, so an aircraft body made from them is lighter to lift.

items.stem: Duralumin is an alloy of aluminium with copper and magnesium. Its density is 2.8 g/cm3 and it is harder than pure aluminium. A titanium alloy has a density of 4.5 g/cm3 and is harder than duralumin. Which is the better choice for a lightweight bicycle frame that must not bend?

options.text: Titanium alloy, because it is the harder of the two
Duralumin, because it is far less dense and still hard
Titanium alloy, because a denser metal is always stronger
Pure aluminium, because it is stronger than any alloy

items.why: The frame must be light, and 2.8 g/cm3 is well below 4.5 g/cm3, while duralumin is still harder than pure aluminium.

items.stem: Soda-lime glass is made by heating a mixture of which substances?

options.text: Sand with boron trioxide, heated strongly
Sand on its own, melted in a hot furnace
Sand, sodium carbonate and limestone
Clay, limestone and sodium chloride

items.why: Most of the glass we use is soda-lime glass, made by heating a mixture of sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.

items.stem: How does borosilicate glass differ from soda-lime glass?

options.text: It melts at a much lower temperature
It is made from pure sand and nothing else
It melts easily once it gets hot enough
It melts at a higher temperature

items.why: Borosilicate glass, made from sand and boron trioxide, melts at higher temperatures than soda-lime glass.

items.stem: How are clay ceramics such as bricks and pottery made?

options.text: Wet clay is shaped and then heated in a furnace
Clay is melted and poured into a cold mould
Dry clay powder is pressed and left to set
Clay is mixed with sand and melted down

items.why: Clay ceramics, including pottery and bricks, are made by shaping wet clay and then heating in a furnace.

items.stem: LD and HD poly(ethene) are both produced from ethene. Why do they have different properties?

options.text: They are built from two different monomers
A different catalyst and conditions are used
HD poly(ethene) is pressed hard after it is made
The HD chains contain a second element

items.why: The properties of polymers depend on the monomer and on the conditions under which they are made, so the same ethene gives two different materials.

items.stem: Why do thermosoftening polymers melt when they are heated?

options.text: The strong covalent bonds along the chains break
Any solid will melt if it is heated enough
Separate chains are held only by weak forces
The polymer is a liquid that was frozen

items.why: The chains are separate and tangled, with only weak forces between them, so they slide apart when heated.

items.stem: Why do thermosetting polymers keep their shape when they are heated?

options.text: They only melt above about a thousand degrees
The covalent bonds in the chains never break
They contain no carbon that could be melted
Cross-links join the chains to each other

items.why: The chains in a thermosetting polymer are joined by cross-links, so they cannot slide apart and the polymer does not melt.

items.stem: Most composites are made of two materials. How are those two materials arranged?

options.text: A matrix surrounds and binds together fibres or fragments
Two materials are melted into a single new substance
Fibres surround the matrix and hold it firmly in place
Two elements are joined chemically to give a compound

items.why: Most composites are made of a matrix or binder surrounding and binding together fibres or fragments of the reinforcement.

items.stem: Which of these materials is a composite?

options.text: Brass, which is copper mixed with zinc
Concrete, gravel held together by cement
Poly(ethene), made from many ethene units
Soda-lime glass, made by melting sand

items.why: Concrete is a composite: cement is the matrix and the gravel is the reinforcement.

items.stem: A table gives: aluminium alloy, density 2.7 g/cm3, does not shatter; soda-lime glass, density 2.5 g/cm3, shatters when dropped; carbon fibre composite, density 1.6 g/cm3, does not shatter. Which material is lightest for a given volume and survives being dropped?

options.text: Soda-lime glass, since glass is the lightest here
Aluminium alloy, since a metal can never break
The carbon fibre composite, the least dense
Aluminium alloy, as it is the densest one

items.why: At 1.6 g/cm3 it is the least dense of the three, and the table says it does not shatter.

items.stem: A saucepan handle must not soften on the hot hob and must not conduct heat well. Which material is most suitable?

options.text: A polymer with strong covalent chains
A toughened soda-lime glass
A hard-wearing steel alloy
A thermosetting polymer

items.why: Thermosetting polymers do not melt when heated and, being polymers, are poor conductors of heat.

items.stem: Which object is most likely to be made from bronze?

options.text: A church bell cast in one piece
A trumpet played in a school band
A knife blade that stays sharp
A drinks can pressed from thin sheet

items.why: Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, is used for bells, statues and ornaments.

items.stem: What is high carbon steel used for?

options.text: Car body panels and sheeting
Cutlery and kitchen sinks
Cutting tools and sharp blades
Aeroplane bodies and frames

items.why: High carbon steel is strong but brittle, which suits cutting tools and blades.

rounds.name: The Haber process and NPK fertilisers

items.stem: What is manufactured directly by the Haber process?

options.text: Ammonia, which is then used to make nitrogen fertilisers
Ammonium nitrate, ready for spreading onto farm fields
Nitrogen and hydrogen, made by breaking down ammonia
Nitrogen and hydrogen, drawn straight from the air

items.why: The Haber process manufactures ammonia, and that ammonia is used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers.

items.stem: Which pair of gases are the raw materials for the Haber process?

options.text: Nitrogen and oxygen gas
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Hydrogen and water
Hydrogen and oxygen

items.why: The specification states that the raw materials for the Haber process are nitrogen and hydrogen.

items.stem: A student is asked to give a source of the nitrogen used in the Haber process. Which answer is correct?

options.text: It is obtained from the air, together with the hydrogen
It is obtained by heating ammonium salts in large vessels
It is obtained from the air, which is about 78% nitrogen
It is obtained by electrolysis of concentrated brine

items.why: Air is the source of the nitrogen and is about 78% nitrogen by volume.

items.stem: Which is the usual industrial source of the hydrogen used in the Haber process?

options.text: Electrolysis of water, which splits it into elements
The air, as hydrogen is one of the gases present in it
Heating ammonia so that it splits into its elements
Natural gas, which consists mainly of methane

items.why: Hydrogen is obtained from natural gas (methane) or from other hydrocarbons.

items.stem: Which conditions are used in the Haber process?

options.text: An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 20 atmospheres
An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres
A nickel catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres
An iron catalyst, 45 degrees C and 20 atmospheres

items.why: The specification gives an iron catalyst, a high temperature of about 450 degrees C and a high pressure of about 200 atmospheres.

items.stem: What is the effect of the iron catalyst in the Haber process?

options.text: It increases the yield of ammonia formed at equilibrium
It only speeds up the reaction at 450 degrees C or above
It speeds up the rate at which the equilibrium is reached
It stops the ammonia formed from breaking down again

items.why: The catalyst raises the rate of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium arrives sooner.

items.stem: The Haber reaction is reversible. What does this mean inside the reactor?

options.text: All the nitrogen and hydrogen react, then some ammonia breaks down
The reaction runs forwards during the day and backwards at night
The ammonia formed can never break down once it is made
Some of the ammonia breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen

items.why: The specification states that the reaction is reversible, so some of the ammonia produced breaks down again.

items.stem: Which equation for the Haber process is written as the specification gives it?

options.text: nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ammonia
ammonia ⇌nitrogen + hydrogen
nitrogen + hydrogen → ammonia
nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonium

items.why: This is the word equation exactly as the specification states it, with the double arrow for a reversible reaction.

items.stem: Which balanced symbol equation represents the Haber process?

options.text: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ NH3
N2 + H2 ⇌ NH3

items.why: Two nitrogen atoms and six hydrogen atoms appear on each side, so the equation is balanced.

items.stem: The mixture leaving the reactor is cooled. What happens?

options.text: The nitrogen and the hydrogen liquefy and are then drawn off
All three gases liquefy together and are then distilled
The ammonia decomposes back to nitrogen and hydrogen
The ammonia liquefies and is removed from the gas mixture

items.why: On cooling, the ammonia liquefies and is removed, leaving the other two gases behind.

items.stem: What happens to the nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted?

options.text: They are recycled back through the reactor
They are burnt to provide heat for the reactor
They are released into the air as harmless gases
They are cooled and sold as by-products

items.why: The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled, so the raw materials are not wasted.

items.stem: A graph shows the rate of the Haber reaction against temperature at a fixed pressure. What does it show?

options.text: The rate falls steadily as the temperature is increased
The rate rises as the temperature is increased
The rate falls as the temperature rises because the yield falls
The rate is highest at the lowest temperatures on the graph

items.why: Higher temperature means more frequent and more energetic collisions, so the rate increases.

items.stem: A graph shows the percentage yield of ammonia against pressure at 450 degrees C. What is the trend, and why?

options.text: Yield falls, because squashing the gases hinders the reaction
Yield is constant, because pressure only changes the rate
Yield falls, because ammonia is squeezed back into its elements
Yield rises, because there are fewer gas molecules in the ammonia

items.why: Four molecules of gas become two, so raising the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.

items.stem: Inside a sealed Haber reactor at equilibrium, what is true?

options.text: Both reactions are still going on at the same rate
Both the forward and reverse reactions have stopped
The amounts of all three gases are now equal
Only the forward reaction is taking place

items.why: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates, so amounts stay constant.

items.stem: Ammonia is removed from the mixture as it liquefies. What is the effect on the equilibrium?

options.text: There is no effect, since the ammonia has already been made
It shifts towards the ammonia side, so more gas reacts
It shifts back towards the nitrogen and hydrogen instead
It stops the reverse reaction from happening at all

items.why: Removing a product moves the equilibrium to replace it, raising the overall conversion.

items.stem: Why is the Haber process not run at a much lower temperature than 450 degrees C?

options.text: Because the yield of ammonia would be lower at low temperatures
Because the iron catalyst does not work at all below 450 C
Because the reaction would then be far too slow to use
Because a lower temperature would shift the equilibrium back

items.why: A low temperature gives a better yield but so slow a rate that the plant would be uneconomic.

items.stem: What is meant by the trade-off between rate of production and position of equilibrium?

options.text: The conditions give the most ammonia per day, not the best yield or the fastest rate
The conditions chosen are simply those that give the fastest possible reaction
The conditions chosen are the ones giving the highest possible yield of ammonia
The catalyst is chosen so that the yield and the rate can both be maximised

items.why: A compromise temperature accepts a lower equilibrium yield in exchange for a workable rate of production.

items.stem: Why is a pressure of about 200 atmospheres used rather than a far higher one?

options.text: Because a higher pressure would reduce the yield of the ammonia made
Because the iron catalyst is destroyed above 200 atmospheres
Because stronger plant, more energy and greater risk cost more
Because 200 atmospheres gives the greatest possible yield

items.why: Yield would rise further, but the extra pipework, compression energy and hazard are not worth the gain.

items.stem: The nitrogen for the Haber process is taken from the air. Which reason best explains this choice?

options.text: Nitrogen taken from the air is more reactive than nitrogen from a tank
Air is free and is about 78% nitrogen, so it is the cheapest source
Air already contains all the hydrogen that is needed for the reaction
Nitrogen from the air needs no purification before it is used

items.why: Commercial conditions and raw materials are chosen for availability and cost, and air costs nothing.

items.stem: An NPK fertiliser contains compounds of which three elements?

options.text: Nitrogen, phosphorus and krypton, symbol K
Nitrogen, potassium and carbon, from K
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium salts
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium

items.why: NPK fertilisers contain compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

items.stem: Why is an NPK fertiliser described as a formulation?

options.text: Because it is one single compound whose formula contains all three elements
Because it uses only insoluble salts so the rain cannot wash it away
Because it is a mixture of salts blended to give set percentages of N, P and K
Because it is made in one reactor from a single mined raw material

items.why: NPK fertilisers are formulations of various salts containing appropriate percentages of the elements.

items.stem: Ammonia from the Haber process can be used to manufacture which substances?

options.text: Ammonium salts and nitric acid
Ammonium salts and sulfuric acid
Nitric acid and sulfuric acid
Nitric acid and a compound called NPK

items.why: The specification states that ammonia can be used to manufacture ammonium salts and nitric acid.

items.stem: Which of these fertiliser raw materials are obtained by mining?

options.text: Phosphate rock and ammonium nitrate, but not the potassium salts
Nitric acid and phosphate rock, but not the potassium salts
Only phosphate rock, since the potassium salts are made in plants
Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock

items.why: The specification lists these three as obtained by mining.

items.stem: Why can phosphate rock not be used directly as a fertiliser?

options.text: Because the rock must be dried out before it is spread
Because the phosphate compounds in it do not dissolve
Because the rock must first be ground into a much finer powder
Because it dissolves so readily that the rain washes it away

items.why: Plant roots take up dissolved ions, so the insoluble phosphate must first be made into soluble salts.

items.stem: Phosphate rock is treated with sulfuric acid. What is produced?

options.text: Calcium sulfate only, with the phosphate left in the rock
Calcium phosphate only, known as triple superphosphate
Ammonium sulfate, which supplies nitrogen and sulfur
Single superphosphate: calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate

items.why: Treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid gives single superphosphate, a mixture of the two salts.

items.stem: Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid. Which products are formed?

options.text: Ammonium nitrate and calcium oxide
Phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate
Calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate
Calcium nitrate and calcium oxide

items.why: Treating phosphate rock with nitric acid produces phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate.

items.stem: Which salt is produced when phosphate rock is treated with phosphoric acid?

options.text: Calcium phosphate, called triple superphosphate
Calcium sulfate, the salt in single superphosphate
Calcium phosphate mixed with some calcium sulfate
Ammonium phosphate, made from the rock alone

items.why: Phosphoric acid converts phosphate rock into calcium phosphate, known as triple superphosphate.

items.stem: A student makes ammonium sulfate in the laboratory by titration and crystallisation. How does industrial production of the same salt differ?

options.text: It reacts the ammonia with an alkali rather than an acid
It is carried out in exactly the same way, but with larger apparatus
It runs continuously on a large scale, with reactants recycled
It adds phosphorus and potassium to make the compound NPK

items.why: Industrial production is continuous, large scale and integrated, whereas the laboratory prepares a single small batch.

items.stem: In a Haber reactor at 200 atmospheres the rate of production is 9, 21 and 33 tonnes per hour at 350, 450 and 550 degrees C. The percentage yield at the same three temperatures is 55, 28 and 12. What do the data show?

options.text: The rate is highest at 350 degrees C, where the yield is highest
The rate rises with temperature while the yield falls
Both the rate and the yield fall at higher temperatures
The rate and the yield are both highest at 450 degrees C

items.why: The rate figures rise from 9 to 33 while the yield figures fall from 55 to 12.

items.stem: At 450 degrees C the rate of ammonia production is 12 tonnes per hour at 100 atmospheres, 24 at 200 atmospheres and 45 at 400 atmospheres. What do these data show?

options.text: The rate falls as the gases are squashed up
The rate stops rising beyond 200 atmospheres
Raising the pressure does not change the rate
Doubling the pressure roughly doubles the rate

items.why: 12 to 24 and 24 to 45: each doubling of the pressure roughly doubles the rate of production.
